newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Little effect on float seen from Telstra dividend.
newsitem.headline: Little effect on float seen from Telstra dividend.

text.p: Telecommunications carrier Telstra Corp Ltd's A$3.0 billion special dividend payment to its owner the Australian government is unlikely to have much affect on the carrier's planned float or 1996/97 profit, analysts said.
Telstra will fund the dividend by raising A$3 billion by June 30 through syndicated loans, which would push up the company's interest costs through a higher debt to equity ratio.
However, analysts said more debt and less equity for Telstra means a lower cost of funds, which should have a minor effect on the company's valuation or potential sale price.
Analysts agreed with Communications Minister Richard Alston's and Finance Minister John Fahey's statement that Telstra's capital structure would be more in line with international telecom companies.
They said the higher debt would push the debt to equity ratio to around 45 percent, from about 30 percent currently.
"It is now not a lowly geared balance sheet, it is a reasonably geared balance sheet," Mullholland said.
Telstra is expected to earn about a A$2.8 billion net profit before abnormals in the year to June 30 1997, from A$2.1 billion a year ago. Analysts said this forecast could change mildly.
Analysts said the government might receive as much as A$1 billion less from its plan to sell one-third of Telstra through a public share offer by the end of 1997.
Estimates of the government proceeds from Telstra's partial privatisation have ranged from A$8 billion to A$11 billion.

"They (the government) get A$2 billion extra, because they get a billion less, arguably, from the float," one telecom analyst said. "But they are getting it four to six months before its floats so they get the interest on that as well," he said.
He said Telstra's overall valuation would be reduced due to having less cash on hand.
Analysts said the government was the big winner out of the deal, which they equated to a share-buy-back.
"I think it is the A$3.0 billion that nobody will ever know went missing," said one analyst, who asked not to be named.
"It is the hand in the cookie jar in the middle of the night, it just disappears," he said.

Standard and Poor's in its ratings downgrade also changed the carrier's outlook to negative from stable, due to the increased competitive threat from the deregulation of the local telecommunications industry from July 1, 1997.
